title: Huawei says AI chip demand outstrips supply as it accelerates its Nvidia challenge
excerpt: At its Huawei Connect conference in Shanghai, the Chinese giant unveiled 2027 AI chip launches and an architecture it claims lets a million processors work as one computer — while admitting it cannot make enough chips for China alone.
body:
• Rotating chairman Eric Xu said on Thursday that Huawei "cannot produce enough artificial-intelligence computing equipment to meet demand in China" and has no plan to expand internationally in a fully-fledged way.
  • Huawei will launch two AI semiconductors in 2027: the 960DT for model training in the first quarter and the Ascend 960PR for inference in the third quarter, with the Ascend 970 and 980 following in 2028 and 2029.
  • Fellow rotating chairman David Wang unveiled the "Peerium" computing architecture and UnifiedBus interconnect, which Huawei claims lets a million processors operate as one computer; the company says a 256,000-card Atlas 950 SuperCluster is already being deployed.
  • Xu claimed Ascend's share of China's AI chip market is bigger than Nvidia's — without providing data — as U.S. export controls keep pushing Beijing toward self-sufficiency.

Huawei Technologies cannot make enough artificial-intelligence computing equipment to satisfy demand inside China and is limiting overseas sales, rotating chairman Eric Xu said on Thursday, as the Chinese giant stepped up its challenge to Nvidia with new chip launches and an architecture it claims lets a million processors work as one computer.

Speaking at the Huawei Connect conference in Shanghai, Xu said testing of Huawei's Ascend 950DT AI chip had produced good results and that the company was in extensive discussions with Chinese AI model developers, many of which he expects to begin training models on systems using the chip next year. "Since we don't have enough capacity to even satisfy the demand in China, we don't have a plan to expand into the international market in a fully-fledged way," Xu told reporters. Huawei supplies some countries where demand is particularly strong, he said, but volumes remain limited.

Two new chips for 2027

Rotating chairman David Wang announced that Huawei will launch the 960DT in the first quarter of 2027 and the Ascend 960PR in the third quarter, according to Reuters reporting from the conference. The Ascend 960, originally expected in the fourth quarter of 2027, has been readied ahead of schedule with twice the performance of existing products, Wang said, according to Chinese outlets including Kechuangban Daily. Further chips are mapped out for the rest of the decade: the Ascend 970 in 2028 and the Ascend 980 in 2029.

Xu also said reliable data on Nvidia's share of China's AI chip market was difficult to obtain — then offered his own estimate anyway: "I think Ascend market share should be bigger than Nvidia's." Huawei did not provide data to support the claim.

The million-processor pitch

The more ambitious reveal was architectural. Huawei announced the Peerium Computing Architecture — which its own website describes as "making one million processors work as one computer" — built around a UnifiedBus interconnect that links CPUs, NPUs, memory, SSDs, network interface cards and switches over a single open protocol. Huawei has developed 11 semiconductors based on UnifiedBus technology, Wang said, and its largest linked systems — called superclusters — can support up to a million AI processors. The company has shipped more than 1,000 smaller linked systems, called supernodes, to more than 370 customers, Wang said.

"We cannot accept a destiny where we cannot control our fate being determined by others in terms of willingness to sell chips to China or not."

— Eric Xu, Huawei rotating chairman, at Huawei Connect in Shanghai

Xu explicitly linked Huawei's chip push to China's drive for self-sufficiency: "No matter if it's for the Chinese government, industry in China, or for Huawei, it is certainly the way forward to try to push for full self-sufficiency for chips." Guo Ping, chairman of Huawei's supervisory board, put the ambition more bluntly to new employees, telling them "Huawei's goal is to become Nvidia," according to Chinese media cited by the Seoul Economic Daily.

The numbers behind the boasts

Independent analysts urge caution. A U.S. council report cited by TrendForce estimates that even under optimistic assumptions, Huawei's AI chip output would amount to roughly 5% of Nvidia's total AI computing power in 2025, falling to 2% by 2027 — and that Huawei will struggle to build the multi-rack systems it markets in meaningful numbers without access to advanced chipmaking tools. The gap, the report argues, is effectively impossible to close given Nvidia's scale, and manufacturing without EUV lithography equipment keeps advanced-node yields uncertain. The context is unforgiving: Huawei has faced U.S. trade restrictions since May 2019, and Washington has tightened export controls on advanced computing chips and semiconductor manufacturing equipment since 2023.

Why this matters for the diaspora

The chip race lands directly on the Indian professionals who staff the world's AI labs and semiconductor firms — including Nvidia itself. Washington's export controls and Beijing's self-sufficiency drive are redrawing where AI talent and capital flow, and India's own chip ambitions, from design to fabrication, are being shaped by the same contest. For Indian engineers in Silicon Valley, Huawei's acceleration is the competitive pressure that will define their industry's next decade.

What's next

Watch whether Chinese model developers actually begin training on Ascend 950DT systems next year as Xu predicted, whether the accelerated Ascend 960 ships on its new timeline, and how Beijing's reported orders for top Chinese tech firms to halt Nvidia purchases evolve. Huawei also plans to open-source its UB-Mesh interconnect protocol — a bid to turn its connectivity approach into an industry standard rather than a proprietary moat.
